title: Ingesting from Message Buses and Cloud Storage, and Applying Changes Incrementally

concepts.heading: Kafka Offsets, Checkpoints and Poison Messages
concepts.body: The Kafka source returns key and value as binary plus topic, partition, offset and timestamp, so deserialization is your job with from_avro, from_json or from_protobuf. The startingOffsets option only decides where a new query starts. A restarted query resumes from the offsets in its checkpoint and ignores the option, so switching latest to earliest on a running query does not backfill anything. To recover a gap, start a second bounded query with its own checkpoint, explicit starting offsets at the start of the gap and an AvailableNow trigger, and write idempotently so overlap with the live stream causes no duplicates. Changing the subscribed topics, the number or type of sources, the stateful operators or the sink type generally needs a new checkpoint, while filters, rate limits and trigger intervals are safe edits. from_avro defaults to FAILFAST, so one corrupt payload fails the batch again after every restart. In PERMISSIVE mode corrupt records become NULL, and rows with a NULL result but a non-NULL value go to a dead-letter table with topic, partition and offset.

concepts.heading: Kinesis and Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics
concepts.body: Each Kinesis shard supports a fixed number of GetRecords calls per second, shared by every polling reader. Several queries reading one stream in polling mode therefore see ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded and a rising iterator age, and a larger cluster does not help because the limit sits on the shard. Databricks advises that a query be the only consumer of a stream. When several queries each need all records, use enhanced fan-out, which gives every registered consumer dedicated throughput per shard. A registered consumer adds Kinesis charges, so set requireConsumerDeregistration to true or manage consumers yourself. Specify either streamName or streamARN, never both, and do not switch between them on an active query, because the checkpoint stores per-shard offsets for the source as identified by its options; restarting can duplicate or lose records, so cut over with a new query, a fresh checkpoint and an idempotent sink. The Pub/Sub connector has exactly-once semantics only for rows it receives from the subscriber. Pub/Sub can still publish duplicates when producers retry, and each copy gets its own messageId, so deduplicate on a business key such as event_id after setting a watermark, using dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Formats and Hidden Files with Auto Loader
concepts.body: Auto Loader handles JSON, CSV, XML, Parquet, Avro, ORC, text and binary files, with schema inference and evolution. XML has no inherent record boundary, so the rowTag option is required and names the element that is read as one row. For a file shaped as orders containing many order elements, rowTag is order. Using the root element would give one row per file holding an array of orders. File sources also skip hidden names: ignoredPathSegmentRegex defaults to ^[._] and is matched against each directory and file name below the path being read, so a partner file named _2026-11-01_orders.csv is listed in storage but never ingested, and a directory whose name matches excludes its whole subtree. The fix is to rename the file or change the regex. Setting an empty string disables the filter, and then marker files such as _SUCCESS can be read too, so a more precise pattern is safer. These behaviors explain most reports of files that exist but never arrive, and they are checked before suspecting notifications, permissions or the checkpoint.

concepts.heading: Applying Change Feeds and Snapshots to Delta and Iceberg Readers
concepts.body: Change events arrive late, out of order and duplicated, so apply them by a sequence, not by arrival. AUTO CDC takes a key, a SEQUENCE BY column and SCD type 1 or 2, and SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(event_ts, event_id) breaks ties on the second field. With hand-written MERGE, the source must have at most one row per target row or the statement fails, so a micro-batch reading the change data feed should drop update_preimage rows, keep the highest _commit_version per key and use a delete clause for _change_type delete. An at-least-once log source is deduplicated inside the batch, then merged insert-only with a predicate on the partition column, such as the last seven days, so the merge prunes files. For nightly snapshots without change flags, one MERGE combines WHEN MATCHED AND changed, WHEN NOT MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE. The change data feed is transient: old versions disappear with log cleanup and VACUUM, so a stale startingVersion fails and the target must be rebuilt from a snapshot. For Iceberg readers of a Delta target, UniForm needs column mapping, and deletion vectors must be purged with REORG first.

examPoints: A question about a Kafka backfill after changing startingOffsets is testing that the option applies only to a new query, so the answer is a separate bounded query with its own checkpoint and an idempotent sink.
A question about throttling with several Kinesis readers is testing enhanced fan-out, and a question about Pub/Sub duplicates is testing deduplication on a business key within a watermark.
A question on out-of-order or repeated CDC events is testing a sequence column with a tie-break in AUTO CDC, or one source row per key in MERGE, and the transient nature of the change data feed.

quiz.q: A Kafka stream started with startingOffsets set to latest and a checkpoint lost two days of events to a parsing bug. An engineer changes the option to earliest and restarts the same query, but the gap is not filled. What should be done?
choices: Run a bounded query with a new checkpoint and offsets at the gap start, writing idempotently
Delete the checkpoint folder of the live query and restart it with earliest, so all retained topic history replays into the table
Keep the checkpoint and set failOnDataLoss to false, which makes the running query reread the gap automatically
Raise the trigger interval of the live query, because a longer interval lets it catch up on the skipped offsets
quiz.explain: startingOffsets is read only when a query starts without a checkpoint, so the restart resumed from the recorded offsets. A separate bounded query with its own checkpoint reads just the gap, and an idempotent write avoids duplicates. Deleting the checkpoint replays everything and duplicates rows.

quiz.q: A CDC feed delivers events for the same customer out of order, and two events can share one event_ts but have increasing event_id values. A pipeline must keep the newest state per customer without history. Which AUTO CDC configuration fits?
choices: Keys on customer_id, SCD type 2, and SEQUENCE BY event_ts alone, with ties resolved by arrival order
Keys on customer_id, SCD type 1, and SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(event_ts, event_id)
Keys on event_id, SCD type 1, and SEQUENCE BY customer_id so every event becomes its own row
No sequence column, because AUTO CDC applies events in the order the micro-batches arrive
quiz.explain: Type 1 keeps only the latest row per key, and a STRUCT sequence orders by event_ts first and event_id on ties. Type 2 would keep history, and ordering by arrival gives wrong results for late events.

recap: Kafka startingOffsets applies only to a new query, so backfill with a separate bounded query and checkpoint; FAILFAST poison messages need PERMISSIVE plus a dead-letter table. Kinesis needs enhanced fan-out for several readers, Pub/Sub needs business-key deduplication, Auto Loader needs rowTag and an eye on hidden-name filters. CDC is applied by sequence, not arrival, and the change data feed is transient.

title: Lakeflow Connect CDC from Relational Databases: Gateway, Source Setup and Failure Recovery

concepts.heading: Gateway and Pipeline: Two Components, Two Modes
concepts.body: A gateway-based database connector, such as the SQL Server connector, has two parts with different rules. The ingestion gateway extracts snapshots and change logs from the source. It runs on classic compute and must stay in continuous mode, because the source keeps its logs only for a retention period and a stopped gateway lets changes expire. Do not stop it manually. Each start also provisions a virtual machine, so restarts are slow. The ingestion pipeline applies the extracted changes to the destination streaming tables and runs on serverless compute, and continuous mode is not supported for it. It is run on a schedule or triggered, and Databricks recommends at least five minutes between runs because serverless startup takes time. This split gives a cost design for a few minutes of freshness: keep the gateway running and schedule the pipeline every few minutes, instead of paying for a continuously running pipeline. Databricks tracks what was extracted and applied, so a failed run resumes at that point without data loss, but only while the logs still exist on the source. If they expired, the affected tables need a full refresh.

concepts.heading: Preparing the Source: Change Tracking, CDC and Keys
concepts.body: The connector reads a change feed that SQL Server itself maintains, so the source is prepared before any pipeline runs. Change tracking records that a row changed, not the sequence of operations, requires a primary key and adds little load. Change data capture records every operation and keeps a history. Databricks recommends change tracking for any table with a primary key to minimize load on the source, and if both are enabled the connector uses change tracking. A managed connector must apply updates and deletes, so it needs a key for every table. It uses the primary key first, then a unique key or unique index, and otherwise treats all columns except large objects as a bundled key. Rows that are identical in all of those columns are ingested as a single row, so a table such as audit_events with true duplicates loses rows in the destination. The repair is a surrogate unique key or unique index on the source, then a refresh of that table. Choose CDC instead when a table has no primary key and a unique index can not be added, accepting higher source overhead.

concepts.heading: Availability Groups and Failover
concepts.body: How the change feed behaves after a source failover decides whether ingestion resumes cleanly. With change tracking, the tracking data is not replicated to secondary nodes, so any change of source node, including an Availability Group failover, requires a full refresh of all tables in the pipeline. With CDC, the log sequence number checkpoints are portable across replicas. If the connector connects through the Availability Group listener address, the pipeline can resume after an unplanned failover without data loss. So the setting that must survive failovers favors CDC through the listener, even though change tracking is lighter for single-node sources. Connect to a specific replica name and the portability is lost. The same logic applies to maintenance: anything that interrupts the gateway for longer than the source log retention, or moves the source to a new node under change tracking, ends in a full refresh. Exam wording like unplanned failover, without a full refresh of all tables points at CDC with the listener; wording like lowest overhead with primary keys points at change tracking.

concepts.heading: Schema Changes, Dropped Tables and Who Can Set It Up
concepts.body: Database connectors handle schema changes in a defined way. A new column is picked up on the next pipeline run unless you opt out, and new tables appear if you ingest a whole schema. A column deleted at the source is not dropped in the destination. A table property marks it inactive so history stays queryable, and if a different column later appears with the same name, the pipeline fails on that table until you drop the inactive column manually or run a full refresh. Renames and data type changes need a refresh as well. When a source table is deleted, the destination table is not deleted either. You drop it manually, which differs from Spark Declarative Pipelines, where removing a dataset from the code removes it from the pipeline objects. For setup there are two models. In the single-user model an admin does everything. In the multi-user model an admin prepares the source with a dedicated ingestion user and creates a Unity Catalog connection that stores the credential, and non-admin engineers use it to create gateway-pipeline pairs without ever seeing the password.

examPoints: A question about freshness of a few minutes at lowest cost is testing a continuously running gateway on classic compute with a short schedule for the serverless ingestion pipeline.
A question about change tracking versus CDC is testing primary keys and source load, and one about unplanned Availability Group failover is testing CDC through the listener.
A question about a gateway stopped longer than log retention is testing that changes are gone and a full refresh is required, and one about identical rows is testing the key the connector picks.

quiz.q: A product team wants SQL Server changes in Delta tables within a few minutes at the lowest cost that still meets this. An engineer proposes switching the ingestion pipeline to continuous mode and stopping the gateway overnight. Which design is right?
choices: Run the gateway continuously on classic compute and schedule the serverless ingestion pipeline every few minutes
Stop the gateway overnight, run the pipeline continuously, and restart the gateway each morning to save cost
Run the ingestion pipeline continuously and schedule the gateway every few minutes, since pipelines read the logs
Replace the gateway with a nightly full refresh of all tables, which avoids depending on source log retention
quiz.explain: The gateway must stay continuous so changes are not lost to source log retention, and it runs on classic compute. The ingestion pipeline applies staged changes and is scheduled. Stopping the gateway risks expired logs and a full refresh.

quiz.q: A company runs SQL Server in an Availability Group. After an unplanned failover, ingestion must resume without a full refresh of all tables. Which setup gives that?
choices: Change tracking on all tables, connecting to the primary replica by its own host name
Change data capture, connecting through the Availability Group listener address
Change tracking, because its data is replicated to secondary nodes automatically
Either feed works, because the gateway rebuilds the change history after any failover
quiz.explain: CDC log sequence checkpoints are portable across replicas, and the listener address lets the pipeline resume. Change tracking data is not replicated to secondaries, so a node change forces a full refresh of all tables.

recap: Gateway on classic compute, always continuous; ingestion pipeline serverless, scheduled. Change tracking is light and needs primary keys; CDC survives Availability Group failover through the listener. Expired source logs mean a full refresh. Dropped columns turn inactive, dropped source tables stay in the destination, and a Unity Catalog connection lets non-admins create pairs.

title: OpenSharing, Clean Rooms and Lakehouse Federation with Governance

concepts.heading: Choosing the OpenSharing Protocol
concepts.body: OpenSharing (called Delta Sharing in older docs) has two protocols, both served by the OpenSharing server built into Databricks. Databricks-to-Databricks shares data and AI assets with recipients that have a Unity Catalog-enabled workspace. It adds notebook sharing, volume sharing, model sharing, Unity Catalog governance, auditing and usage tracking on both sides, and works across accounts, clouds and regions. Databricks-to-Open shares tabular data with users on any platform, such as Power BI or Python, without a workspace. So a partner who needs a table, a volume of PDF files and a notebook must be a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient. For Databricks-to-Open recipients the provider chooses the authentication. A bearer token is a long-lived credential file the recipient must store securely, while OIDC federation lets the recipient identity provider issue short-lived tokens that Databricks validates, which suits security teams that reject stored long-lived tokens. On the consuming side of a Databricks-to-Databricks share, granting access is not enough: a metastore admin or privileged user must create a catalog from the share, and then analysts get ordinary Unity Catalog privileges on it.

concepts.heading: Share Versus Clean Room
concepts.body: A normal share gives the recipient read access to the provider data, so the recipient sees the rows and can run any code on them. It fits distribution. A clean room fits two or more parties that must combine sensitive data without direct access to each other raw records, such as an advertiser and a retailer computing customer overlap and conversion per campaign. Each party shares tables with the central clean room, an isolated Databricks-managed environment, using OpenSharing, and approved notebook code runs there on serverless compute. Collaborators review and approve the code before it touches the data. Safeguards matter for the exam. After creation a clean room is locked down, so no new collaborators can join, and a third company means creating a new clean room with all three. Each clean room is limited to ten collaborators. Because the code runs on serverless compute, data in a storage-firewalled bucket cannot be reached by default. Options are default storage, allowing the serverless compute in the network rules, or enabling SecureConnect for the clean room so firewalled storage is reachable without allowlisting that network.

concepts.heading: Lakehouse Federation: Query and Catalog Federation
concepts.body: Lakehouse Federation exposes external systems as Unity Catalog foreign catalogs. A connection stores the path and credentials, and a foreign catalog mirrors the external database. There are two kinds. Query federation targets relational databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server through JDBC, with pushdown so the query runs partly in the remote system and partly in Databricks. It is read-only and suits ad hoc reporting and proofs of concept. Which operators go remote is a documented list per source: for PostgreSQL filters, projections, limits and aggregates are pushed down, but a window function runs on Databricks compute. Catalog federation connects external catalog platforms such as Hive Metastore or AWS Glue, and queries read the files directly in object storage and run only on Databricks compute, using a connection, a storage credential and an external location. That is the fast path to query Glue-registered tables from Unity Catalog during a staged migration. Neither kind writes: an INSERT into a foreign catalog fails, so publishing results to PostgreSQL needs a JDBC write in a job or another tool.

concepts.heading: Governing Federated Access and When to Ingest Instead
concepts.body: Federated access has two layers that must both allow a query. Unity Catalog privileges on the foreign catalog, schema and table decide which Databricks principals may query. The connection uses one shared database login, so that login decides what can be read at all, and end users never use their own database logins. Finance can therefore be granted only the ledger schema and marketing only another schema with ordinary grants on one foreign catalog, but if the database user lacks rights on a schema, a Unity Catalog SELECT still ends in a permission error that originates in the source. Dedicated access mode compute has an exception: you must own the underlying connection to query the foreign catalog, and CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG on it is not enough, while standard access mode and serverless use normal privileges. Federation sends every query to the source, so a growing operational dashboard loads the production database. When concurrency and volume grow and the source supports it, ingest with a Lakeflow Connect managed connector into Delta tables and point the dashboard at them.

examPoints: A question sharing tables, volumes and notebooks with a partner is testing Databricks-to-Databricks, and one with a vendor without a workspace that bans long-lived tokens is testing Databricks-to-Open with OIDC federation.
A question where neither party may see raw records and both review code is testing a clean room; a third collaborator later means a new clean room, and firewalled storage means SecureConnect.
A question on slow dashboards over a foreign catalog is testing ingestion with Lakeflow Connect, and one on INSERT into a foreign catalog is testing that federation is read-only.

quiz.q: A retailer wants to give a logistics partner a Unity Catalog table, a volume of PDF delivery notes and an explanatory notebook. The partner has its own Unity Catalog-enabled Databricks workspace. Which sharing approach fits?
choices: Databricks-to-Open with a bearer token, because tokens can carry any asset type and format
Export the files to a bucket and share the table through a view in a clean room
Databricks-to-Databricks, since notebooks and volumes need a Unity Catalog recipient
A foreign catalog on the partner side, which federates the retailer's volumes and notebooks
quiz.explain: Notebook and volume sharing are supported only by the Databricks-to-Databricks protocol with a Unity Catalog-enabled recipient. Databricks-to-Open shares tabular data, and a foreign catalog is read-only federation of external databases, not a sharing mechanism.

quiz.q: A federated PostgreSQL query filters orders to one month, sums amount per customer, then ranks customers with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC). Which statement describes where the work happens?
choices: Everything is pushed down because query federation runs the whole statement inside PostgreSQL
Nothing is pushed down, since foreign catalogs always copy tables to Delta before querying
The window function is pushed down, while the filter and the aggregate run on Databricks compute
Filter and aggregate go to PostgreSQL, while the window function runs on Databricks
quiz.explain: Query federation pushes down only a documented list of operators. Filters, projections and aggregates are on the list for PostgreSQL, while window functions are not, so ranking runs on Databricks compute.

recap: Databricks-to-Databricks carries notebooks, volumes and models; Databricks-to-Open serves any platform, with OIDC for short-lived tokens. Clean rooms combine data without exposing rows, are locked after creation and need SecureConnect for firewalled storage. Federation is read-only, governed by Unity Catalog grants plus the shared database login, and heavy dashboards should use ingested Delta tables.

title: Advanced Spark SQL and PySpark: Window Frames, Grouping Analytics, Joins and Approximate Aggregates

concepts.heading: Window Frames: Defaults, Ties and Forward Fill
concepts.body: A window function computes a value per row from a frame of related rows without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does. PARTITION BY isolates groups, ORDER BY sequences them, and the frame limits which rows are visible. When the window has an ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default is RANGE from unbounded preceding to the current row, and rows with equal ordering values are peers that fall into the frame together. Two consequences follow. First, last_value over that default frame returns the current row, or the last of its ties, so showing the final status of an order on every row needs ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Second, a running SUM ordered by a timestamp with ties gives tied rows the same total, and switching to ROWS makes each row a step but leaves the order among ties undefined, so totals can change between runs. Add a unique tie-breaker to ORDER BY. Forward fill of sparse sensor data uses last(temp, true) over PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, where true ignores NULLs, with no self-join.

concepts.heading: Ranking, QUALIFY and Top-N Inside Aggregates
concepts.body: Ranking functions treat ties differently. For revenues 100, 100, 90, 80, 70 in descending order, row_number gives 1 to 5 and splits ties arbitrarily, rank gives 1, 1, 3, 4, 5 and skips numbers, dense_rank gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, and ntile(3) buckets rows by position, not by value. So the three highest distinct revenue values per category, with ties kept, is dense_rank less than or equal to 3. QUALIFY filters on window results without a wrapping subquery: SELECT ... QUALIFY dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) <= 3. When the requirement is one row per key holding the latest N values as an array, with no window function and no self-join, max_by(expr, ordExpr, limit) in a plain GROUP BY returns an ARRAY of up to limit values from the rows with the largest ordering values; limit is an INT from 1 to 100,000, rows with a NULL ordering value are excluded, and ties on the cutoff make the result non-deterministic.

concepts.heading: Grouping Analytics and Join Semantics
concepts.body: ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS compute several aggregation levels in one pass. In a subtotal row the rolled-up column shows NULL, which looks identical to a source NULL, so a row with region EU and channel NULL is ambiguous. Select grouping(channel), which is 1 when the column was aggregated away and 0 for real values including NULL,, or grouping_id for several columns. For joins, an outer join keeps unmatched left rows with NULLs on the right, and a WHERE predicate such as x.year = 2026 runs after the join and is never true for NULL, so unmatched stores vanish and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an inner join. A condition that restricts the right table belongs in the ON clause, while WHERE suits conditions on the final result. Range joins match a value to an interval and can use binning. If the condition also has an equality on a numeric column, the optimizer may bin that column too and lose performance, so cast numeric equality keys to STRING on both sides so only the range condition is optimized.

concepts.heading: Approximate Aggregates at Scale
concepts.body: Distinct counts are not additive: a user active on Monday and Tuesday counts once for the week but once per day in the daily numbers, so summing stored daily counts overstates weekly uniques, exact or approximate. The fix is to store a mergeable sketch. hll_sketch_agg builds a HyperLogLog sketch as a compact BINARY value suitable for a table column, hll_union_agg merges the sketches of several days, and hll_sketch_estimate returns the approximate distinct count of the union. The error depends on lgConfigK, from 4 to 21 with default 12, and sketches to be merged need compatible settings. For percentiles over billions of rows, exact percentile must hold the distinct values per group and can run out of memory. approx_percentile(expr, percentile, accuracy) avoids sorting everything: accuracy is a positive integer defaulting to 10000, higher values cost more memory, and 1.0 divided by accuracy is the relative error. Accuracy 100 means about 1 percent error, 1000 about 0.1 percent, and the default about 0.01 percent. A target of 0.02 percent therefore needs at least 5000, and the default meets it.

examPoints: A question where last_value returns the current row is testing the default RANGE frame with ORDER BY, fixed with an explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame.
A question about the top three distinct values with ties is testing dense_rank with QUALIFY, and one about the latest N values as an array per key is testing max_by with a limit.
A question about weekly uniques from daily counts is testing HyperLogLog sketches with hll_union_agg, and one on a LEFT JOIN losing rows is testing ON versus WHERE.

quiz.q: A report uses GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, channel) and shows a row with region EU and channel NULL. Analysts disagree whether it is a subtotal or EU sales with no channel recorded, because the source also contains NULL channels. How should the query separate the cases?
choices: Select grouping(channel): 1 for rolled-up rows, 0 for real values including NULL
Replace NULL channels with a text value before the ROLLUP, so subtotal NULLs stay unique
Filter the output with WHERE channel IS NULL, which keeps only the subtotal rows
Use CUBE instead of ROLLUP, because CUBE never reports NULL in subtotal rows
quiz.explain: grouping() distinguishes a rolled-up column from a source NULL. Replacing NULLs first merges real unknowns into one label, which changes the data, and CUBE also reports NULL for aggregated columns.

quiz.q: A daily job stores COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) per site and day over billions of events. Product now needs weekly and monthly unique users per site, and summing the daily counts overstates the result. What is the best design?
choices: Sum the stored daily approx_count_distinct values, which become exact once added across a week
Store hll_sketch_agg(user_id) per site and day, then merge the period with hll_union_agg and estimate
Recompute COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) from the raw events for every weekly and monthly query, with no stored state
Store the daily counts in a materialized view, since the view merges overlapping users
quiz.explain: Distinct counts do not add up. Mergeable HyperLogLog sketches stored per day can be unioned for any period and estimated. Recomputing from raw events works but is costly, and a view over counts cannot know which users overlap.

recap: Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE to current row, so last_value needs an explicit frame and running totals need a unique tie-breaker. dense_rank plus QUALIFY handles tied top-N, max_by with a limit handles top-N arrays, grouping() labels subtotals, ON versus WHERE protects outer joins, and mergeable sketches and approx_percentile accuracy handle scale.

title: VARIANT for Semi-Structured Data and AI Functions such as ai_query in Pipelines

concepts.heading: Querying VARIANT: Paths, Case and Special Characters
concepts.body: Databricks recommends VARIANT over JSON strings for semi-structured data. Query syntax looks similar, with col:field, dot notation, brackets and a cast such as ::int, but several semantics differ and can break queries after a migration. All VARIANT path elements are matched case-sensitively, while JSON string queries are case-insensitive, so payload:Customer_ID returns NULL when the stored key is customer_id. The [*] syntax is not supported, and VARIANT encodes NULL differently. The dot operator selects a sub-field, so a key that contains a period, colon, space or bracket must be escaped: raw:['zip.code'] reads the field named zip.code, while raw:zip.code means field zip then sub-field code. To turn an array into rows, use a lateral variant_explode, which returns pos, key and value; for an array key is NULL and value is one element, still a VARIANT, so cast it: SELECT o.id, i.value:sku::string, i.value:qty::int FROM orders o, LATERAL variant_explode(o.payload:items) i. Input that is NULL or not an array or object yields no rows. Because the inner structure is not declared, schema_of_variant_agg(col) merges the schemas of all rows, including fields found in only some rows, to guide promoting stable fields into typed silver columns.

concepts.heading: Parsing, Nulls, Round Trips and Table Compatibility
concepts.body: parse_json raises an error on malformed input, so one truncated body fails the whole batch. try_parse_json returns NULL instead. The pattern is to parse with try_parse_json, send rows with a NULL result but non-NULL input to a rejects table, and let good rows flow. VARIANT also distinguishes two kinds of null. A missing path returns SQL NULL, so v:coupon IS NULL is true. A key that exists with an explicit JSON null returns a VARIANT holding null, for which IS NULL is false and is_variant_null is true. A data quality check that counts both cases separately uses both predicates. Parsing is not exactly reversible: to_json(variant) does not preserve whitespace, key order is arbitrary and trailing zeros in numbers may be truncated, so keep the raw STRING when you must prove the exact received text. For Delta tables, a table created with a VARIANT column has the feature enabled, and an existing table uses the table property delta.feature.variantType set to supported. Enabling it upgrades the writer protocol, which can break external Delta clients that do not support it.

concepts.heading: ai_query in Batch Pipelines: Scale, Errors and Structure
concepts.body: AI Functions are built for set-based, large-scale use from SQL, notebooks, Lakeflow pipelines and jobs. They manage parallelization, retries and scaling, so Databricks advises submitting the full dataset in one query instead of manually splitting it into slices in a Python loop. With ai_query, use Databricks-hosted foundation model endpoints for batch work. By default failOnError is true, so one endpoint error on a row fails the entire query and discards the work. With failOnError set to false each result becomes a STRUCT with the parsed response and an errorMessage, the response is NULL on failure, and failed rows can be selected and retried later. Chat models given only a prompt may wrap JSON in prose, which breaks a downstream from_json on a few percent of rows. The responseFormat argument, for chat foundation models, enforces the output shape with a DDL string such as STRUCT of vendor, total and due_date, or a JSON schema. The modelParameters struct, for settings such as max_tokens and temperature, must hold constant values, not data-dependent ones, so a per-row limit taken from a column is rejected; run separate queries per limit.

concepts.heading: Task-Specific Versus General Functions, Governance, Cost and Images
concepts.body: AI Functions come in two kinds. Task-specific functions such as ai_translate, ai_summarize or ai_classify cover one task with Databricks-managed approaches and no customization, and Databricks recommends them for getting started. ai_query is the general-purpose function for custom prompts and chosen models. Governance differs by kind. Unity Catalog EXECUTE on the system.ai schema controls the task-specific functions: by default everyone has it, and an admin can remove it and grant EXECUTE on approved functions as an allow-list. That does not govern ai_query, which calls a Model Serving endpoint, so endpoint permissions control it. For cost, the compute running the query is always billed, and ai_query is billed for the endpoint you specify. Inference on Databricks-hosted endpoints is recorded in system.billing.usage with product MODEL_SERVING and offering type BATCH_INFERENCE, which includes ai_query workloads and can be joined to job metadata to rank jobs by LLM spend. For images, read files with read_files as binaryFile and pass files => content to a vision model; supported image inputs are JPEG and PNG, so convert other formats such as TIFF first.

examPoints: A question where a VARIANT query returns NULL after a migration from JSON strings is testing case-sensitive paths, and a key with a period is testing bracket escaping such as raw:['zip.code'].

A question about malformed JSON failing a nightly job is testing try_parse_json plus a rejects table, and one about proving exact received text is testing keeping the raw string because parse_json is not exactly reversible.

A question about errors in a large ai_query run is testing failOnError set to false, one about unreliable JSON output is testing responseFormat, and one about governance is testing that ai_query is controlled by endpoint permissions.

quiz.q: A batch job runs SELECT id, ai_query('databricks-llama', 'Summarize: ' || text) FROM tickets over 8 million rows. A few hundred rows hit endpoint errors and the whole query fails, discarding hours of work. The team wants the other rows to complete. What should they do?
choices: Wrap the call in a Python loop over 5,000-row slices so a failing slice is skipped on its own
Add failOnError => false, so each result is a struct and failed rows can be retried
Set modelParameters with a smaller max_tokens for each row so the endpoint stops returning errors
Switch to a task-specific function, which cannot fail because it ignores endpoint errors on each row
quiz.explain: failOnError false returns a struct with the response and an error message, so failures are isolated per row and retried later. Manual slicing fights the built-in parallelism and retries, and per-row model parameters must be constants.

quiz.q: A governance team removed EXECUTE on the system.ai schema from all users and granted it back for only ai_translate and ai_summarize. Analysts can still run ai_query against a hosted foundation model. Why?
choices: The EXECUTE grant on system.ai is cached for a day, so ai_query keeps working until the cache expires
ai_query is a task-specific function and therefore inherits EXECUTE from the other two granted functions
Metastore admins automatically hold EXECUTE on every function, and the analysts share that role
Those grants do not govern ai_query, which calls a serving endpoint with its own permissions
quiz.explain: The system.ai allow-list applies to the task-specific functions. ai_query calls a Model Serving endpoint, so access is controlled by permissions on that endpoint.

recap: VARIANT paths are case-sensitive, escape special characters with brackets, flatten arrays with variant_explode, parse tolerantly with try_parse_json, keep raw text for proof and mind the writer protocol upgrade. ai_query runs in one set-based query, uses failOnError false for isolation, responseFormat for structure, constant modelParameters, endpoint permissions for governance and MODEL_SERVING BATCH_INFERENCE for cost.

title: Data Quality Expectations in Lakeflow Pipelines: Actions, Quarantine, Failures and Metrics

concepts.heading: Three Actions and How to Choose Them
concepts.body: An expectation is a SQL boolean constraint evaluated on each record of a flow. Expectations apply to streaming tables, materialized views and views, and have three actions. Warn, the default expect, keeps invalid rows and records pass and fail counts. Drop, expect_or_drop, removes invalid rows from the target and logs how many were dropped, but the rows themselves are gone. Fail, expect_or_fail, stops the update when invalid records are unacceptable. A good rollout for a new source is to start with plain expect to measure how bad the data is, then switch the stable rules to expect_or_drop after a month, and reserve fail for cases such as a broken primary key where continuing is worse than stopping. In SQL every expectation is its own named clause: CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, where leaving out ON VIOLATION means warn and the other action is FAIL UPDATE. Python adds grouped decorators expect_all, expect_all_or_drop and expect_all_or_fail that take a dictionary, which has no SQL equivalent, so SQL authors repeat the clause per rule.

concepts.heading: Quarantine and Portable Rules
concepts.body: None of the three actions stores invalid rows separately, yet compliance often requires keeping them with a reason. The documented quarantine pattern keeps every row in one table with a boolean flag. You build a rule set and a quarantine condition, NOT(rule1 AND rule2), then add an is_quarantined column in a table that uses expect_all so metrics are still recorded. One view with is_quarantined false feeds the gold layer, and another view with true feeds the review process. Bad data stays available without polluting downstream tables. When the same eight rules apply to 25 datasets and change monthly, Databricks recommends storing expectation definitions separately from pipeline logic. A rules Delta table with name, constraint and tag columns, plus a helper such as get_rules(tag) that returns a dictionary, is passed to a decorator such as expect_all_or_drop. Tags group the rules, reuse is consistent across pipelines, and changes are audited as table changes without editing code. This portable pattern is a Python technique because the grouped decorators are Python only.

concepts.heading: What a Failed Expectation Does
concepts.body: Expectations enforce quality inside a flow; they are not orchestration. In a triggered pipeline a failed fail-expectation fails and rolls back only that flow's update, and other parallel flows continue independently, so a validation materialized view with expect_or_fail does not stop a downstream table from refreshing. In a continuous pipeline the failure stops the flow and all dependent flows, and the pipeline emits a message with the reason. The update is rolled back atomically and manual intervention is needed: fix the pipeline code so it handles the invalid data, then restart. For real gating, split validation and downstream work into separate pipelines and coordinate them with control flow between the pipeline tasks in Lakeflow Jobs. To find the offending record, remember that fail expectations modify the query plan so the violating record can be tracked. The update fails with an EXPECTATION_VIOLATION message naming the violated expectations and including the input data and the output record, which works for many queries but not all. Fail actions record no pass and fail metrics.

concepts.heading: Metrics, the Event Log and Limits
concepts.body: Metrics for warn and drop actions are recorded in flow_progress events of the pipeline event log, which is also the source for the Data quality tab. For some flows a COMPLETED event does not contain the metrics, because they are reported per micro-batch in flow_progress events with status RUNNING, so a sum over COMPLETED rows alone misses counts. Streaming tables and materialized views created in Databricks SQL are backed by a standalone pipeline. They support CONSTRAINT expectations, but the Data quality tab of the pipeline UI is not available for them, so query the event log instead. Metrics are also absent when no expectations are defined, when an update had no new data, or when the operator or flow type does not support expectations, for example some sinks. Expectations are not supported with AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT: a constraint on that target gives neither enforcement nor metrics, so put the check on a downstream dataset that reads the dimension. Constraints must be valid SQL conditions, evaluated per record to true or false.

examPoints: A question that must keep bad rows for review but keep them out of gold is testing the quarantine pattern with an is_quarantined flag and two views, because drop, warn and fail do not store invalid rows separately.
A question where a downstream table still updated after expect_or_fail is testing that a triggered pipeline rolls back only the failing flow, while a continuous pipeline stops dependent flows too.

A question about missing metrics is testing flow_progress events with status RUNNING, the missing Data quality tab for standalone SQL pipelines, or the lack of expectation support in AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT.

quiz.q: A streaming table receives trip records. Rows with a NULL pickup or dropoff zip must not reach gold reports, but compliance requires keeping them for review with the reason. Which design in a Lakeflow pipeline meets both needs?
choices: Use expect_or_drop on both columns and read the dropped rows from the pipeline event log later
Use expect_or_fail so the pipeline stops, then repair the rows by hand before restarting
Flag rows as is_quarantined using expect_all, then expose valid and invalid rows as two views
Use plain expect and filter the invalid rows in every downstream query with its own WHERE clause
quiz.explain: The documented quarantine pattern keeps all rows with a flag so valid rows feed gold and invalid rows feed review. The event log holds counts and not the dropped rows, and fail stops everything.

quiz.q: A triggered pipeline has a validation materialized view with expect_or_fail on a primary key check. The check fails, yet a downstream table in the same pipeline still refreshed. The team expected it to be blocked. What explains this?
choices: The expectation was evaluated at the end of the update, after downstream tables had already committed
The pipeline was set to development mode, in which expectation failures never stop other flows
Only the failing flow is rolled back in a triggered pipeline; validation tables do not gate others
Fail expectations act only in continuous pipelines, so in a triggered one the action silently becomes warn
quiz.explain: In a triggered pipeline a failed expectation rolls back only that flow, and other flows continue independently. Gating needs separate pipelines coordinated with control flow.

recap: Warn measures, drop removes, fail stops. Quarantine with a flag when bad rows must be kept, portable rules tables and expect_all decorators in Python, one named CONSTRAINT per rule in SQL. Triggered pipelines roll back only the failing flow, continuous ones stop dependents. Read metrics from flow_progress including RUNNING events, and put checks after AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT.
